title: Permissionless circuit-breaker activation silently stops working for oracles that have no next price
content:
A.1.10.3.2.4 gives the liquidations circuit breaker four graduated levels — from Level 0 (liquidations enabled) through Level 3 (no new liquidations, no resets, no bidding) — and, notably, "allows for **permissionless activation** of the circuit breaker, if the price decrease in a collateral exceeds a preset percentage value between oracle price updates," tripping Level 2 "because both new auctions and resets reference the current oracle price."

The trigger condition is `next_oracle_price < current_oracle_price * breaker_price_tolerance`, with the tolerance currently 0.5 (A.1.10.3.2.4.1, A.1.10.3.2.4.1.1) — a halving between updates trips the breaker without anyone deciding.

Then the quiet sentence: "In instances where the price oracle model does not support the price delay function, **the permissionless activation of the liquidation circuit breaker ceases to function, since there is no next oracle price**."

The mechanism depends on a two-value comparison that only delayed oracles provide. For collateral using an oracle without a next-price stage, the automatic protection simply does not exist — and nothing about the breaker's configuration would show that. The parameter is set, the contract is deployed, the level is 0; the trigger is just unreachable.

This is the more dangerous class of failure than an outage, because it produces no signal. Governance can still trip the breaker manually via the CLIPPER_MOM path, so the collateral is not undefended — but the fast, automatic, human-independent layer is absent precisely for the oracle types where nobody has been told to look.

The practical implication is that the effective coverage of this safeguard is a function of which oracle model each collateral uses, and that mapping is not recorded alongside the breaker's parameters.
description: A.1.10.3.2.4.1 notes that where the price model lacks a delay function the automatic trigger 'ceases to function', so an automated safeguard has a failure mode that raises no alarm.
